content    Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure     INTRODUCTION  nMunicipalities have   Constitutional responsibility for providing sustainable and viable  nwater services to the communities within their areas of jurisdiction
nThe purpose of these guidelines is to assist municipalities undertake the development of  nwater and sanitation infrastructure  with   focus on the design aspects of development
nFurther guidelines are in the process of being developed for Water Services Development  nPlans  social aspects and operation and maintenance of water services projects

Purpose of guidelines  nIt is important to note that these guidelines     uf   ARE MERELY INTENDED TO GIVE GUIDANCE TO MUNICIPAL nOFFICIALS  PLANNERS AND DESIGNERS    uf   Are not intended to replace professional expertise and engineering judgement    uf   Provide overarching guidance and cannot be used as   replacement for nspecifications    uf   Must be used together with recognised standards  codes  and acts such as those of nthe South African Bureau of Standards  SANS Codes   the Water Services Act  nthe National Water Act  and the Occupational Health and Safety Act  nThese guidelines are made available through two media     uf     CD has been distributed which contains this document as well as   number of nuseful folders
The contents of the folders are listed at the end of this document    uf     downloadable version of the document is also accessible from the web page of nthe Department of Water Affairs and Forestry

The DWAF web page also ncontains the same folders that are included on the CD Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure               Definitions of minimum norms and standards      nThe aim of Water Services projects funded out of government grants is primarily to  nprovide   basic level of water services
nSection   of the  Strategic Frame work for Water Services  provides the  minimum  ntechnical norms and standards for water services
The Strategic Framework is included in  nthe Legislation and Policy Folder

nThe following definitions and minimum standards are given in the Strategic Framework       nBasic water supply facility  is   nThe infrastructure necessary to supply   litres of potable water per person per day  nsupplied within   metres of   household and with   minimum flow of   litres per  nminute  in the case of communal water points  or      litres of potable water supplied  nper formal connection per month  in the case of yard or house connections

nBasic water supply service  is   nThe provision of   basic water supply facility  the sustainable operation of the facility    available for at least   days per year and not interrupted for more than   consecutive  nhours per incident  and the communication of good water  use  hygiene and related  npractices

nBasic sanitation facility  is   nThe infrastructure necessary to provide   sanitation facility whic   is safe  reliable   nprivate  protected from the weather and ventilated  keeps smells to the minimum  is easy  nto keep clean  minimises the risk of the spread of sanitation  related diseases by  nfacilitating the appropriate control of disease carrying flies   nd pests  and enables safe  nand appropriate treatment and or removal of human waste and wastewater in an  nenvironmentally sound manner

nBasic sanitation service  is   nThe provision of   basic sanitation facility which is easily accessible to   household  the  nsustainable operation of the facility  including the safe removal of human waste and  nwastewater from the premises where this is appropriate and necessary  and the  ncommunication of good sanitation  hygiene and related practices

nPotable water quality  is   nWater supplied by water services providers intended to be used for drinking or domestic  npurposes  potable water  must be of   quality consistent with SANS    Specifications  nfor Drinking Water   as may be amended from time to time
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure   Metering and flow control    nAll unrestricted water connections must be metered or controlled to   basic level

Where  nappropriate  water services providers should consider the benefits of offering households  ncontrolled flow connections  for example  yard tanks  that can provide   basic supply of  nwater cost effectively
Where pre payment meters are installed  these must take into  naccount the free basic water services policy and allow for access to   basic amount of  nwater at zero tariff
nEradication of bucket toilets   nThe bucket system is an unsuitable and inappropriate level of service
All water services  nauthorities must identify and implement programmes for the eradication of all bucket  nsystems by

Project development life cycle  nA typical project development life cycle consists of the following phases   nEstablishment of institutional arrangements  nThe designated municipality is the water services authority and is responsible for water  nservices provision
The water services authority either contracts with   water services  nprovider or fulfils that function itself

nPlanning phase  nThe municipality     uf   prepares   Water Services Development Plan  WSDP  as part of its Integrated nDevelopment Plan  IDP  for the area of jurisdiction of the Water Services nAuthority  WSA     uf   undertakes Feasibility Studies for each water or sanitation project identified in the nWSDP  nDWAF integrates all WSDPs into   National Reference Framework
nDesign phase  nThe municipality procures the design consultant who designs the works and prepares the  ntender documentation or the municipality does it in house
nTender stage  nAdvertising  site inspection  adjudication of tenders received and award of contract

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure        Construction phase      nExecution of the works in accordance with the tender documentation under supervision      nOperations and maintenance      nThe Water Services Provider operates and maintains the works  with or without the  nassistance of contractors  and collects the revenue
nThe Water Services Authority  WSA  monitors the Water Services Provider  WSP  and  nmanages   he contract that it has with the WSP
nThe WSA undertakes an annual water services audit and reports to DWAF who performs  nthe function of Regulator

Legislation affects all phases of  ndevelopment  and for example stipulates requirements for taking water from the resource   nfor the planning of water services  how to determine institutional arrangements  and th    nrequirements for financial and other reporting

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure             INSTITUTIONAL ARRANG EMENTS              Introduction      nThe following institutions are responsible for the supply of water and sanitation services      uf    The Water Services Authority      uf    The Water Services Provide    Sometimes   Water Board or bulk water provider    nand    uf    The Department of Water Affairs and Forestry as regulator
For example DPLG  nmanages the Municipal Infrastructure Grant and the Equit able Share and the Department  nof Health has an important function regarding health and hygiene and sanitation
nA Water Services Authority  WSA  is the municipality that has been designated  nresponsibility for ensuring access to water services
The WSA is   oth the owner of the  nworks and is the elected representative of the customers
nA water services provider  WSP  is the person or organization that actually provides  nwater services to consumers or to another water services institution
The WSA can either  nappoint   WSP  for example another municipality    water board or   private contractor   nor can fulfil the function itself

Deciding on and contracting with   water services provider      nThe WSA should follow the procedure set out in     of the Municipal System   Act when  ndeciding whether it should fulfil the WSP function itself or whether it should contract  nwith   separate WSP
model Terms of Reference for       Assessment has been  ndeveloped by the Municipal Infrastructure Unit  MIU  which is associated with   BSA
nThis model Terms of Reference is included in the Institutional Folder
nS   of the Water Services Act sets out requirements that must be complied with when    nWSA contracts with   WSP
The Minister has promulgated regulations under     of the  nWater Ser vices Act which sets out the minimum requirements with which   contract  nbetween   WSA and   WSP must comply

nEven if the WSA fulfils the WSP function itself  it should account separately  for water  nservices       it should   Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure         uf    keep separate financial accounts of how much was spent on or invested in water  nservices during each financial year      uf    the revenue it received from the sale of water services      uf    funds received from National Government and   ther sources that were allocated  nto water services etc

Model Bylaws that comply with the requirements of     of  nthe Water Services Act are included in the Legislative and Policy Folder

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure             PLANNING              Introduction      nWater and sanitation projects are essentially planned at three levels      uf    At the nation al level the Department of Water Affairs and Forestry  DWAF   nmaintains   national reference framework      uf    At   municipal level each Water Services Authority  WSA  compiles and  nregularly updates   Water Services Development Plan  WSDP   and     uf    At   project level each WSA undertakes   feasibility study for each project and  ncompiles   technical report

nThis hierarchy of plans are discussed below            National reference plan      nThe Department of Water Affairs and Forestry is required to comment on the Water  nServices Deve lopment Plans  WSDP  of each WSA and to ensure that all current and  nprojected activities are compatible with the national strategies

To enable   common  nframework for assessing WSDPs    National Reference Plan is being developed which  nwill capture the ess ence of each WSDP in one common structure that relates water  nservices planning to the National Water Resource Strategy  Catchment Management  nStrategies  together with water allocations and licensing   Provincial Strategies and IDPs

nMunicipalities will need to cross reference their plans to the National Reference  nFramework in order  to integrate their own planning with other developments being  nundertaken in surrounding areas

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure               Water services development plan      nSections   to   of the Water Services Act    requires   Water Services Authority to  nprepare   Water Services Development  Plan
These sections describe how to develop and  nadopt   WSDP and sets out the contents of the WSDP
nThe Water Services Act    is included in the Legislation and Policy Folder
nWhilst the WSDP is   legal requirement  the real value of preparing   WSD   lies in the  ndevelopment of   plan whereby the key municipal water services targets are set for   five  nyear period
nThe WSDP forms   subset of  and must be aligned to  the municipality   Integrated  nDevelopment Plan  IDP
nThe Department of Water Affair   and Forestry has prepared   set of Guidelines for  npreparing   WSDP
These Guidelines provide basic information about the WSDP  as  nwell as specific information on how to prepare the WSDP

Under the Municipal  nInfrastructure Grant  MIG  it is no longer necessary for municipalities to submit business  nplans to National Governm ent for approval

nThe size of the dam is dependent on the water demand  the required assurance of  ndelivery  the hydrological characteristics of the river  and the characteristics of the dam  nbasin

Weirs      nWhere   dam is used for bulk water storage  and the water is released down the river  it  nmay be necessary to construct   weir at  the point of abstraction
The purpose of the weir  nis usually to provide limited balancing storage for the bulk releases from the dam

nWeirs can also be constructed to store limited amounts of runoff  or even  by allowing the  nbasin to be filled with alluv ial material  to create   reservoir within the alluvial sand from  nwhich water can be abstracted
nIn the case of weirs  siltation is   far greater problem than in the case of large or medium  nsized dams
The outlet works and abstraction points of weirs need  to be kept free of silt
nWeirs  generally being of   limited height and capacity  will also be overtopped by  large   nfloods
They will therefore need to be constructed of concrete or other non  erodable  nmaterial
nA site for   weir  where both the riverb ed and the abutments consist of good quality rock  nis an ideal situation
More usually the weir is founded on rock in the river section and one  nor both of the abutments will comprise of soft river  bank materials
In this case special  nmeasures are required     prevent outflanking of the structure by  large  floods

General   nThe suitability of plumbing materials in low cost housing units has to be viewed from the  nperspe ctive of pricing  its water saving capabilities  durability and the risk of it being stolen for its  nscrap value
nAn important item  although not material related  is the location of water meters in low cost  nhousing schemes
Often  where the meter is locat ed on lot  accessibility for reading purposes is  ncompromised when occupants later erect high fences  for security reasons
The best position  nfor the meter is outside the property  in an undercover  location on the footway  or vertically  nmounted  against the   welling very effective for low coat housing

However  provision has been made in the by  law for Council to  nuse pipes  fittings and other plumbing components  which are not on the Jaswic list  should this  nbe required in order to evaluate the suitability of new materials for spec ific applications
Pipes and piping systems for underground use in the supply of potable  nwater
nAn important part in the installation of water pipes in underground locations  is the condition of  nthe soil in which the pipe is to be laid
If it is con taminated with chemical substances  this could  naffect the durability of the pipe
It would also determine the material of which the pipe is  nmanufactured
Copper      nCopper pipe is historically the preferred material in the Cape Town region
For underground use  only class is allowed   nbecause of its thicker wall
Class   pipe is however  much more expensive than the other    nclas
Copper pipe should not be laid in soil that contains ash  salt and chemicals such as  nammonia and magnesite
These substances will cause  pitting  of the wall of the pipe
Polypropylene  polycop            nThis type of  plastic  pipe is very popular for underground use
The Wat er Services Hillstar depot  nhas been using it for the installation of new water connections  ranging in size from   to     mm  since approximately    and it has proven to be very reliable
The brass  Conex   nfittings could prove to be expensive  especial ly in the larger sizes
It should not be laid in soil  nthat is contaminated with petrol  oil and   number of other chemicals
These chemicals  npermeate through the wall of the pipe  resulting in bad taste and smell in the drinking water
In  nsuch cases  the   nly solution is to replace the pipe with class   copper  since the smell and  ntaste lingers and cannot be eliminated  from the plastic pipe
This condition affects all pipes and  nfittings manufactured from plastic polymers  and is therefore not only restricte   to polycop  npiping

nFor this reason  in the case of plans approval for   service station  we call for copper pipe to be  nused in both above ground and underground applications in the forecourt area  where invariably  nspills of oil petrol will take place
nIt is imperative that only SA NS approved  class   polycop pipe is used
It has been found that  nthe lighter class   pipe is not so durable
HDPE  high density polyethylene       nThis plastic pipe has also gained popularity for underground use
Personal experience has shown that with age  underground leaks tend to be problematic
nThis is found to be the case  when we have to process rebate claims for underground defects  non private properties
It has also been fo und that moles have   special affinity for these pipes   nand many an underground leak is due to   hole having been gnawed into the pipe
Other types of  plastic  pipes      nThere is   ho st of other  plastic  pipes and pipe systems for potable water installation on the  nmarket
Of late  these include composite pipes  which combine layers of plastic and Aluminium   nto form   tube
The problems with many of these systems are that special tools are required to  nfacilitate its installation  and that the fittings are not always readily available

Galvanised mild steel pipes      nIt should be noted that in line with our Water services by  law  galvani sed mild steel pipes and  nfittings are not allowed to convey water supplied from the Municipality   mains
nThis is because our water is only chemically stabilised for copper systems
It is also  soft  and  ntherefore aggressive in nature  and re acts with other metallic pipes  such as galvanised steel  nand Aluminium
In the case of      pipes  serious encrustation forms on the inside of the pipes   nthereby diminishing its bore
This eventually causes poor supply pressures and restricted flows  nfrom   erminal fittings
nAccording to the Red Book pipes may have to be above ground due adverse conditions  such  nas rock

When considering laying pipes above ground  the following factors need to be taken  ninto account         uf    Provision should be made for expansion  the effects of thermal changes must be  nconsidered
The supports should be designed to carry  nthe load of the pipe as well as the water it conveys

SYSTEM DESCRIPTION   nUnlike conventional gravity systems which depend solely on gravity flows  vacuum  nsewer systems make use of   combination     gravity and differential air pressure as the  ndriving force that propels sewage through the sewer network
Vacuum sewer systems  nconsist of three key components   collective chambers   vacuum sewers and the vacuum  nstation

nFigure    Major components of vacuum sewer systems      nAs constructed in Kosovo  toilets cubicles at each sanitation block are drained through      mm diameter uPVC pipes to an adjacent vacuum valve pit containing the collection  nchamber  sensor unit and an interfac   valve

Once   predetermined volume of sewage  nhas accumulated in the collection chamber the pneumatically activated sensor unit  nprompts the opening of the interface valve which links the collection chamber to the  nvacuum sewer network
When the interface   alve opens  the sewage  followed by    nshort burst of air  is sucked into the vacuum sewers

Each input of energy  occurring as  nthe each interface valve along the network opens  further propels the sewage along the  nvacuum sewer network  consisting of   to   diameter pipes  until it reaches the  nvacuum station where it accumulates in vacuum vessels

Vacuum pipe  nwork      nCollective  nchambers  Vacuum station        nService Guidelines   Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT                                                      The vacuum station houses the vacuum pumps which generate and maintain the  nnegative pressure in the vacuum vessels and throughout the vacuum sewer network
nThe sewage that accumulates in the vacuum vessels is evacuated by sewage pumps  nand is conveyed to   sewer outfall where it joins an existing gravity sewer
nFigu re    The Saw Tooth method used for the vacuum sewer lines
nFigure    Collective chamber        nService Guidelines   Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT

Advantages   nVacuum sewerage has the advantage of enabling the use of conventional flush toilets  nwithout the  need for deep trenches  large diameter sewers  numerous access manholes  nand the need to always travel in straight lines  as is customary with waterborne  nsewerage

The use of reduced diameter pipelines and shallow trenches in Kosovo  nreduced the disruption caused retrofitting   sewer network in the informal settlement by  nminimizing the number of shacks that had to be moved to allow for construction

Due to  nthe flat gradients  sandy soils and high water  tables in the area  the installation of    nconventional   ravity sewer system would have used   mm diameter pipes installed at  ndepths of up to   and incorporating three lift stations
